class Identity : public Unary#
#include <identity.h>

A pass-through identity node that implements no transformations or operations of its own.

This node operates identically to the base Unary node. Its primary use case is to act as an attachment point for AttributeModifiers without affecting the global coordinate space of the attributes, which is useful when its child node contains an arbitrary transformation.

Public Functions

virtual std::shared_ptr<Node> clone() final#

Clones the node and returns a new instance of the node.

Note

This may be called before or after prepare() is called, however it is always more efficient to call it after. This is because the prepare() function must be called on all clones of the node separately. If you call prepare() first and then clone the node, the clone() operation will copy from memory instead of re-reading from disk.

Returns:

A new instance of the node

The accuracy of the subtree rooted at this node.

class Rotate : public Unary#
#include <rotate.h>

Rotates a child node about the centre of the child’s bounding box by three Euler angles in degrees.

Parameters, always in this order:

  • pitch: angle about the X axis

  • yaw: angle about the Y axis

  • roll: angle about the Z axis

The vec3 constructors pack the same angles as (x, y, z) = (pitch, yaw, roll).

Order: the child is turned by roll about Z first, then by yaw about Y, then by pitch about X. All three turns are about the fixed world axes (through the pivot), so the applied rotation matrix is R = Rx(-pitch) * Ry(-yaw) * Rz(-roll), and a child point c maps to the world point R * (c - p) + p.

Sign: every angle is negated before it is applied, so a positive angle turns the child clockwise when looking from the positive end of its axis toward the origin. This is the opposite of the right-hand rule. For 90 degree turns:

  • Rotate(90, 0, 0) sends +Y to -Z and +Z to +Y.

  • Rotate(0, 90, 0) sends +Z to -X and +X to +Z.

  • Rotate(0, 0, 90) sends +X to -Y and +Y to +X. Use from_axis_angle() for a right-hand-rule rotation about any axis, and matrix() to see exactly what is applied.

Pivot: the rotation turns about the child’s bounding-box centre p, not about the origin. The pivot is fixed the first time bounding_box() runs, so bounding_box() is safe before prepare(), but you must still call prepare() before evaluate() or sample(). Use Transform to rotate about the origin.

Rotation is an isometry, so the child’s signed distance is returned unchanged and stays exact. The sample point in evaluate() and sample() is mapped back into the child by the inverse rotation about the pivot.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy()): an exact child stays exact. A bound child stays a bound only for turns by multiples of 90 degrees; any other turn makes it approximate, because the bounding box is the axis-aligned bounds of the turned child box and a bound only promises the per-axis distance to the child’s own box (see AffineDistance::keeps_axis_alignment()).

How faithfully this node’s value, including its whole subtree, matches the true signed distance.

Composes the node’s own operation with its children’s accuracy, so the root’s answer describes the whole tree. exact and bound promise that the value clamped to the bandwidth is lipschitz_bound()-Lipschitz and that values outside the bounding box are at least the per-axis distance to it (see DistanceAccuracy). Only valid after prepare(); some nodes decide from what prepare()

measured. The default is approximate, so a node without an override can only disable optimizations that rely on the guarantee.

The child’s accuracy, except that a bound child turned off the axes is approximate. An exact child’s value is at least the Euclidean distance to its box, and the turned box lies inside this node’s box, so it stays exact. A bound child only promises the per-axis distance to its own box. Turned by anything but multiples of 90 degrees, a point just off a turned edge can be nearer to the child’s box per child axis than it is to this node’s box per world axis, and the band edge of this node’s box cuts the child’s field off below the band. Returns the 4x4 child-to-world matrix this node applies, pivot included.

Builds a rotation by an angle about an arbitrary axis through the pivot, using the right-hand rule.

A positive angle turns counter-clockwise when looking from the tip of the axis toward the origin, so from_axis_angle((0, 0, 1), 90) sends +X to +Y. The equivalent (pitch, yaw, roll) are stored, so angles() reports them.

class Scale : public Unary#
#include <scale.h>

Scales a child node about the origin, uniformly or per axis.

This node is unary, therefore can only have one child.

The scale is applied when evaluate() is called by mapping the query point into the child’s local coordinates, (x / sx, y / sy, z / sz), and converting the returned signed distance back into world units.

Uniform scaling (one factor, or three equal factors) is exact: the child’s distance is multiplied by the factor, so a true signed distance field stays a true signed distance field.

Non-uniform scaling (different factors per axis) is allowed but warps the distance field, so use it with caution. Equal distances in the child become ellipsoids in the world, and no formula that only sees the child’s value can recover the exact world distance. This node returns the first-order estimate d / |S^-1 n|, where d is the child’s value, n its unit gradient direction (central differences in child space) and S = diag(sx, sy, sz). The estimate is exact on planar faces, exact to first order at the surface, and always lies between d * min(s) and d * max(s). It drifts from the true distance far from curved surfaces, so nodes that read distances away from the surface (Offset, Shell, distance-driven attributes, smooth blends) give approximate results. The sign, and therefore the surface itself, is always exact. Each evaluation costs about seven child evaluations instead of one.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy()): a uniform scale keeps the child’s accuracy and Lipschitz bound; a non-uniform scale is approximate, since its gradient direction can switch between faces and the estimate then jumps.

virtual DistanceAccuracy distance_accuracy() const override#

How faithfully this node’s value, including its whole subtree, matches the true signed distance.

Composes the node’s own operation with its children’s accuracy, so the root’s answer describes the whole tree. exact and bound promise that the value clamped to the bandwidth is lipschitz_bound()-Lipschitz and that values outside the bounding box are at least the per-axis distance to it (see DistanceAccuracy). Only valid after prepare(); some nodes decide from what prepare()

measured. The default is approximate, so a node without an override can only disable optimizations that rely on the guarantee.

The child’s accuracy for a uniform scale; approximate for a non-uniform one. A uniform scale s returns s f(p / s): the band-clipped value is the child’s, clipped to T / s, stretched by s in both value and space, so its Lipschitz bound is unchanged, and the box and its per-axis distance scale by s too. That needs the child prepared with a band of at least T / s, which

prepare() gives it; if the child was last prepared with less (a child shared with another parent) this is approximate. A non-uniform scale returns the first-order estimate, whose finite-difference direction switches between faces on the child’s medial surfaces, so the value jumps there: approximate.

Returns:

The accuracy of the subtree rooted at this node.

Protected Functions

virtual void prepare_impl(const glm::vec3 &voxel_size, double bandwidth) override#

Node-specific part of prepare(), called after the bandwidth has been recorded.

Composite nodes prepare their children here. The base implementation does nothing.

Prepares the child; when shrinking, its bandwidth is widened to bandwidth / min(s). The child returns no value farther than its bandwidth, in its own units, outside its bounding box. Scaled down, that would be closer than this node’s bandwidth in world units, and a union around it would then report a farther sibling’s distance instead. Scales of 1 or more keep the bandwidth as it is. Also sets the finite-difference step used by the non-uniform distance estimate.

Parameters:

  • voxel_size – The size of a voxel we plan to sample with.

  • bandwidth – The bandwidth of the tree we are sampling.

class Transform : public Unary#
#include <transform.h>

Places a child with a full 4x4 affine matrix in one step.

This node is unary, so it may only have one child.

Convention: points are column vectors and the matrix maps child coordinates to world coordinates, world = M * (x, y, z, 1). The matrix acts about the origin (unlike Rotate, which turns about the child’s bounding-box centre). Compose the usual way, M = T * R * S, to scale first, then rotate, then translate. The translation is the last column, M[3] in GLM’s column-major storage. The bottom row must be (0, 0, 0, 1) and the upper-left 3x3 block A must be invertible; reflections (det A < 0) are allowed. shear() and shear_matrix() build a shear.

Distance: if A is a rotation or reflection times a uniform scale s (A^T A = s^2 I), the child’s distance is multiplied by s and stays exact. Otherwise A stretches space unevenly and the signed distance field is warped, so use it with caution. The node then returns the first-order estimate d / |A^-T n|, with d the child’s value and n its unit gradient direction in child space, exactly like a non-uniform Scale. It is exact on planar faces, exact to first order at the surface, and always lies between d times the smallest and the largest singular value of A, but it drifts from the true distance far from curved surfaces. The sign, and so the surface itself, is always exact. That path costs about seven child evaluations per evaluation.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy()): a similarity keeps an exact child exact, and keeps a bound child a bound only when it maps the axes onto the axes (turns by multiples of 90 degrees, axis reflections). Any other matrix is approximate.

virtual DistanceAccuracy distance_accuracy() const override#

How faithfully this node’s value, including its whole subtree, matches the true signed distance.

Composes the node’s own operation with its children’s accuracy, so the root’s answer describes the whole tree. exact and bound promise that the value clamped to the bandwidth is lipschitz_bound()-Lipschitz and that values outside the bounding box are at least the per-axis distance to it (see DistanceAccuracy). Only valid after prepare(); some nodes decide from what prepare()

measured. The default is approximate, so a node without an override can only disable optimizations that rely on the guarantee.

The child’s accuracy through a similarity; approximate otherwise. A similarity A = s Q returns s f(A^-1 (p - t)), which keeps the child’s Lipschitz bound when the child is prepared with a band of at least T / s (

prepare() does this). An exact child stays exact: its value is at least the Euclidean distance to its box, whose image lies inside this node’s box. A bound child only promises the per-axis distance to its own box, which survives only if Q maps the axes onto the axes; otherwise the axis-aligned bounds of the mapped box break that promise, so it is approximate. A matrix that is not a similarity returns the first-order estimate, which jumps where the child’s gradient direction switches between faces: approximate. Approximate also if the child was last prepared with a narrower band than T / s.

Returns:

The accuracy of the subtree rooted at this node.

static glm::dmat4 shear_matrix(const glm::dvec3 &direction, const glm::dvec3 &normal, double factor, const glm::dvec3 &origin = glm::dvec3(0.0))#

Builds the matrix of a shear: points slide along a direction in proportion to their height above a plane.

p’ = p + factor * ((p - origin) . n) * d, with d and n the unit direction and normal. Points on the plane through origin with normal n stay put; a point at height h above it moves factor * h along d. factor is the tangent of the shear angle (the tilt of lines that were parallel to n). A shear keeps volume and is not a similarity, so a Transform built from it returns the first-order distance estimate (see the class details).

Parameters:

  • direction – The direction points slide in; normalized internally.

  • normal – The normal of the fixed plane; normalized internally. Must be perpendicular to direction.

  • factor – How far a point slides per unit of height above the plane.

  • origin – A point on the fixed plane.

Throws:

std::runtime_error – if a vector is zero or not finite, direction and normal are not perpendicular, or factor is not finite.

Returns:

The child-to-world matrix.

namespace AffineDistance#

Converts a child’s signed distance into world units through a linear map that may stretch space unevenly (a non-uniform Scale, a general Transform, or a map Jacobian).

With A the linear map from child to world coordinates, the child field f evaluated at the mapped point is no longer a world distance: equal child distances become ellipsoids in the world. No formula that only sees f can recover the exact world distance, because that depends on where the child’s closest surface point lies. The first-order estimate f / |A^-T n|, with n the child’s unit gradient direction, is used instead. It is exact for planar surfaces, exact to first order at the zero level set of any surface, and always lies between f times the smallest and the largest stretch of A. Far from a curved surface it under- or over-estimates. The sign, and therefore the surface itself, is always exact.

bool keeps_axis_alignment(const glm::dmat3 &matrix, double tolerance = 1e-6)#

True if a linear map sends the coordinate axes onto the coordinate axes with one common stretch.

That is a positive multiple of a signed permutation matrix: a turn by multiples of 90 degrees, a reflection across a coordinate or diagonal plane, a uniform scale, or a product of these. Such a map sends an axis-aligned box onto an axis-aligned box and scales the per-axis (Chebyshev) distance to it by the stretch, so a child value that is at least the per-axis distance to the child’s box stays at least the per-axis distance to the mapped box. A general rotation does not keep that: the axis-aligned bounds of a turned box are larger, but a point off a turned edge can be farther from those bounds per axis than it is from the turned box in the child’s own axes.

Parameters:

  • matrix – The linear map.

  • tolerance – Allowed deviation of each entry, relative to the stretch (absorbs rounding from single-precision rotations).

Returns:

True if the map is axis-aligned in this sense.

class Mirror : public Unary#
#include <mirror.h>

Unary node that reflects child geometry across a plane.

A world sample point \(p\) is reflected across the configured plane before evaluating the child. The original child geometry is not retained; use Union(child, Mirror(..., child)) if both the source and reflected copy are desired.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy()): a reflection is an isometry, so an exact child stays exact. A bound child stays a bound across a coordinate plane (or a diagonal plane that swaps two axes) and is approximate across any other plane.

Note

As for every node, call prepare() on the root before evaluate() or sample(); bounding_box() is safe before it.

class MappedNode : public Unary#
#include <mapped_node.h>

Wraps any child node through a CellMap, so geometry designed in a flat box follows a curved, conformal map.

A world point inside the active map domain is inverted to logical map coordinates (u, v, w), scaled to child coordinates c = (u * s_u, v * s_v, w * s_w), and the child is evaluated at c. With Space::physical the scale s is the map’s average size of one logical unit in millimetres along each axis, so the child is authored in approximate millimetres: the child box [0, nu * s_u] x [0, nv * s_v] x [0, nw * s_w] covers the whole map (see child_bounds()). With Space::logical the scale is 1 and the child is authored directly in logical cell units. An explicit per-axis scale may also be given.

Distance: the child’s value is converted to world units with the local map Jacobian. With M = J * diag(1 / s) the derivative of world position with respect to child coordinates, the returned value is the first-order estimate d / |M^-T n|, where d is the child’s value, treated as a distance in child units, and n its unit gradient direction (central differences, or one-sided differences on a medial surface where central differences cancel). The estimate therefore always lies between d times the smallest and the largest stretch of M. It is accurate near the zero level set (the surface that is meshed), so it is safe within a narrow band of a few voxels, but it is an approximation, not a true distance: far from the surface the curvature of the map makes it under- or over-estimate. Where the child has no value (beyond its prepared bounding box) a conservative lower bound from the child’s box distance and a lower bound on the smallest singular value of M is returned instead. distance_accuracy() is approximate.

Domain: the mapped child exists only inside the active map domain. Outside it, or in trimmed regions and holes, the node returns the positive distance to the domain, and inside it the field is clipped with the domain distance, exactly as mapped lattices are. set_clip_to_domain(false) skips that clipping inside the domain, so a wrapped box keeps its own depth there: use it when the node marks a zone of the map (a region for zones, overlap bands or blends) rather than a solid that should end at the domain. Periodic map directions wrap, so a child crossing the seam is cut there.

prepare() prepares the child with the voxel size and bandwidth converted to child coordinates.

virtual DistanceAccuracy distance_accuracy() const override#

How faithfully this node’s value, including its whole subtree, matches the true signed distance.

Composes the node’s own operation with its children’s accuracy, so the root’s answer describes the whole tree. exact and bound promise that the value clamped to the bandwidth is lipschitz_bound()-Lipschitz and that values outside the bounding box are at least the per-axis distance to it (see DistanceAccuracy). Only valid after prepare(); some nodes decide from what prepare()

measured. The default is approximate, so a node without an override can only disable optimizations that rely on the guarantee.

How faithfully the value of the whole subtree matches the true distance: always approximate. The value is the first-order estimate, which can exceed the true distance away from the surface. Its transitions are not continuous either: beyond the child’s prepared box the fallback scales by 1 / |M^-1|_F, which is at most the smallest stretch of M and only 1 / sqrt(3) of it where M stretches evenly, so the clipped field drops there; and just outside the active domain the domain distance (near 0) replaces whatever the mapped child gave just inside.

Returns:

The accuracy of the subtree rooted at this node.

class Warp : public Unary#
#include <warp.h>

Deforms space: the child is sampled at g(p), where a WarpMap g pulls each world point back to the child point it came from.

Attributes (pull-back): the child’s attributes are sampled at g(p), so material follows the deformation. The map’s natural coordinates are available as fields through coordinate_field(): “child_x”, “child_y”, “child_z” for every map, plus the map’s own (for example the twist angle).

Distance: the child’s value f at g(p) is converted to world units with the map’s Jacobian J = dg/dp. With A = J^-1 the local child-to-world map, the value is the first-order estimate f / |J^T n| from AffineDistance (n is the child’s unit gradient direction), as MappedNode and a non-uniform Scale use. The surface is exact; the value is accurate near it and an approximation far from it. Built-in maps have analytic Jacobians; a field map takes central differences, which costs six more map evaluations per point. With a Lipschitz bound L on g (|g(p) - g(q)| <= L |p - q|), the value is f / L instead, never larger than the true distance inside the box for an exact child. Beyond the child’s prepared box the conservative fallback of MappedNode is used: the child’s box distance plus bandwidth, times a lower bound on the stretch of A, or divided by L with a bound. distance_accuracy() is approximate either way, because f / L can fall below the distance to the box just outside it (see there).

Bounding box: a warp moves material, so the box comes from explicit bounds or from the map’s world_bounds() of the child’s box. A map that cannot bound its image (a field map) needs explicit bounds.

prepare() estimates the largest stretch of g over the box (from L, or by sampling the Jacobian) and prepares the child with the bandwidth widened by it. It then lets the map check itself against the prepared child (WarpMap::prepare()).

virtual DistanceAccuracy distance_accuracy() const override#

How faithfully this node’s value, including its whole subtree, matches the true signed distance.

Composes the node’s own operation with its children’s accuracy, so the root’s answer describes the whole tree. exact and bound promise that the value clamped to the bandwidth is lipschitz_bound()-Lipschitz and that values outside the bounding box are at least the per-axis distance to it (see DistanceAccuracy). Only valid after prepare(); some nodes decide from what prepare()

measured. The default is approximate, so a node without an override can only disable optimizations that rely on the guarantee.

How faithfully the value of the whole subtree matches the true distance: always approximate. Without a Lipschitz bound on g the value is the first-order estimate, which can exceed the true distance away from the surface. With a bound L the value f / L is Lipschitz inside the box grown by the bandwidth (the child is prepared with the bandwidth times max(1, L), and the fallback beyond the child’s box clips to the bandwidth like the child’s own “no value”), but nothing keeps it at least the per-axis distance to the box just outside the box: maps that keep lengths across a face the child reaches (the height of a twist or taper, the depth of a bend or wrap) give the distance divided by L there. Where that is still below the bandwidth at the edge of the box grown by the bandwidth, the clipped field jumps to the bandwidth (no value), which no Lipschitz bound covers. See deforming_space_architecture.md.

The accuracy of the subtree rooted at this node.

static std::shared_ptr<Warp> bend(double radius, const std::shared_ptr<Node> &child, const glm::dvec3 &origin = glm::dvec3(0.0), const glm::dvec3 &direction = glm::dvec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0), const glm::dvec3 &axis = glm::dvec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0))#

Bends the child around an axis (BendMap).

The line through origin along direction is bent into a circle of radius |radius| about an axis parallel to axis: toward direction x axis for a positive radius, away for a negative one. Arc length along that line is kept (it is the neutral surface), and the child stays put at the origin. Valid while, on the side it curls toward, the child stays closer to the line than |radius| (farther would pass the bend centre and fold), and within half a turn each way (|length along direction| < pi |radius|). Coordinates: “angle” (degrees, zero at the origin) and “radius” (distance from the bend’s centre line). The box is the exact annular sector holding the child.

Parameters:

  • radius – The bend radius; non-zero, its sign picks the bend side.

  • child – The child node.

  • origin – A point on the line that is bent; it stays put.

  • direction – The direction of the line that is bent.

  • axis – The direction of the bend axis; made perpendicular to direction.

Throws:

std::runtime_error – if the child is null, the radius is zero or not finite, or the directions are zero or parallel.

Returns:

The Warp node.

static std::shared_ptr<Warp> displace(const std::shared_ptr<Vec3Attribute> &displacement, const std::shared_ptr<Node> &child, const std::optional<Box> &bounds = std::nullopt)#

Moves the child’s material by a displacement field (DisplacementMap).

Material at X moves to X + u(X). u is sampled at the undeformed point X, in the child’s coordinates, and is a vector in those coordinates (the Warp’s own: world, when the Warp is the root). The pull-back solves X + u(X) = p by fixed-point iteration, then Newton steps; prepare() throws if u folds material onto itself, and points that fail to converge are counted (failed_inversions()). Coordinate: “displacement” (|u|).

Parameters:

  • displacement – The displacement field u, sampled with d = 0.

  • child – The child node.

  • bounds – The world box of the moved child; std::nullopt to estimate it by sampling u.

Throws:

std::runtime_error – if displacement or child is null.

Returns:

The Warp node.

class Offset : public Unary#
#include <offset.h>

Moves its child’s surface outward (positive distance) or inward (negative distance).

The value is f - t, where f is the child’s signed distance and t the offset distance. The distance may be a constant or a field (a ScalarParameter), so the offset can vary through space. A field is sampled with the child’s signed distance as d.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy(), for the whole subtree): a constant offset of an exact or bound child is a bound with the child’s Lipschitz bound (an offset of an exact distance is exact only on one side of the new surface), outward or inward and for any finite child bound; offset 0 keeps the child’s accuracy. A field offset is an approximation. Its value is divided by 1 + L when the field has a Lipschitz hint L, which keeps the surface and the slope, but the scaled value falls below the distance to the box and short of the bandwidth where the child goes silent.

Attributes: inside the child (removal, or the child’s own material) the child’s attributes apply, with this node’s attributes taking precedence. Material that the offset grows outside the child follows the growth policy: undefined (the default, no attributes), extend (the child’s attributes at its closest surface point) or own (this node’s only). This node’s own attributes (and grown ones) are only evaluated, and attributes only returned, where the offset’s value is 0 or less.

Bounding box: moves out by the largest distance when it is positive. Otherwise it is the child’s box: an inward offset of a child whose value has slope bound L only moves the surface in by |t| / L, so shrinking the box by |t| would cut material. A field distance must have known bounds (ScalarParameter::bounds()).

class Shell : public Unary#
#include <shell.h>

A wall of a given thickness that follows its child’s surface.

With f the child’s signed distance and t the thickness, the wall lies

  • inward (the default): inside the child, -t <= f <= 0, value max(f, -f - t);

  • outward: outside the child, 0 <= f <= t, value max(f - t, -f);

  • centered: across the surface, |f| <= t / 2, value |f| - t / 2. The thickness may be a constant or a field (a ScalarParameter), sampled with the child’s signed distance as d. Where a field thickness is zero or negative there is no wall.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy(), for the whole subtree): a shell with a constant thickness over an exact or bound child, in any direction, is a bound with the child’s Lipschitz bound. The child is prepared t beyond the bandwidth (t / 2 for centered), which covers every child value the clamped wall depends on: down to -(bandwidth + t) for the inner face of an inward wall, up to bandwidth + t for the outer face of an outward one. A field thickness is an approximation: with a Lipschitz hint L the value is divided by 1 + L (1 + L / 2 when centered), which keeps the slope but falls below the distance to the box.

Attributes: the wall inside the child carries the child’s attributes (removal), with this node’s attributes taking precedence. Wall outside the child (outward and centered shells) is grown material and follows the growth policy. This node’s own attributes (and grown ones) are only evaluated, and attributes only returned, where the wall’s value is 0 or less.

Bounding box: an inward shell keeps the child’s box. Outward and centered shells grow it by the largest t (or t / 2), so a field thickness for them needs known bounds.

The legacy constructors take a negative thickness for an inward shell; they also accept a positive one, which means the same inward shell.

class Thicken : public Shell#
#include <shell.h>

Turns a surface or thin body into a solid of thickness t: the value is |f| - t / 2.

A centered Shell under its own name. Use it on a child whose value is an unsigned distance to a surface (an open sheet), or on a thin body to make it thicker. The thickness may be a field with known bounds. Attributes, accuracy and bounding box follow Shell with Direction::centered: the part inside the child keeps the child’s attributes, the rest is grown material and follows the growth policy.

Distance accuracy: a constant thickness over an exact or bound child is a bound with the child’s Lipschitz bound; a field thickness is an approximation (see Shell).

enum class GrowthPolicy#

What attributes a growth operator gives material its child never had.

Growth operators (positive offsets, outward shells, thickening) create material outside their child. Inside the child they always report the child’s attributes; this policy only decides the grown region.

Values:

enumerator undefined#

No attributes in grown material (the historical Offset behaviour).

enumerator extend#

The child’s attributes at its closest surface point, so material carries straight outward.

enumerator own#

Only the operator’s own attributes.

std::optional<AttributeSamples> sample(GrowthPolicy policy, Node &child, const std::shared_ptr<AttributeSet> &own_attributes, double x, double y, double z, double distance, double child_distance)#

Attribute samples for a point in material the operator grew.

The operator’s own attributes always take precedence over the child’s, matching the interior merge. With GrowthPolicy::extend the child is sampled at its closest surface point, found by stepping p - d * n with n the child’s unit gradient. The step is repeated (at most four times) until the child reports material there, so the result does not depend on the child’s distance being exact.

  • child – The prepared child node.

  • y – The y-coordinate.

  • z – The z-coordinate.

  • distance – The operator’s signed distance at the point, passed to its own attributes.

  • child_distance – The child’s signed distance at the point (positive in grown material).

Returns:

The samples, or std::nullopt for GrowthPolicy::undefined and where distance is positive (no material, so no attributes are evaluated).

class Mix : public Binary#
#include <mix.h>

Interpolates two child fields with a spatial weight in [0, 1].

A zero weight returns the left child and a one weight returns the right child. The weight may be an explicit mapped scalar field or a native smooth ramp derived from a prepared region node’s signed distance.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy()): always an approximation. The slope of a varying weight multiplies the (unbounded) difference between the children’s values, and where one child has no value the other is returned unmixed, so even a constant weight jumps at the edge of a child’s band.

class Tile : public Unary#
#include <tile.h>

A tile is a unary operator that repeats a geometry as a pattern in a grid.

Cell k along an axis spans [k c, (k + 1) c), with the child’s origin placed at the cell centre (k + 1/2) c. By default the grid is infinite. An optional per-axis count makes it a finite array of cells 0 … n − 1 along that axis (a count of 0 or less keeps the axis infinite); points beyond the ends see the nearest end copy.

Pull-back node: the child is sampled at the point’s position within its copy, so attributes follow the material. instance_index_field() exposes the copy index as a field, so material can vary per copy.

Neighbours: prepare() measures how far the child’s box overhangs its cell and also evaluates that many neighbouring copies, taking the nearest. A child that fits its cell costs one evaluation.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy()): the value is the nearest copy within that window. It keeps the child’s accuracy only when every copy left out of the window is farther than the band from any point, which prepare() checks from the child’s box: per axis, the window must reach the overhang plus the band (a child that fits its cell must clear every cell face by the band). Otherwise a nearer copy just across a cell face can be missed, even for a child whose box is centred in its cell, and the value is approximate. Copies whose boxes overlap or touch merge, so the nearest copy’s value is then only a bound inside them.

Components are negative while the size is unset; prepare() then derives it from the child.

virtual DistanceAccuracy distance_accuracy() const override#

How faithfully this node’s value, including its whole subtree, matches the true signed distance.

Composes the node’s own operation with its children’s accuracy, so the root’s answer describes the whole tree. exact and bound promise that the value clamped to the bandwidth is lipschitz_bound()-Lipschitz and that values outside the bounding box are at least the per-axis distance to it (see DistanceAccuracy). Only valid after prepare(); some nodes decide from what prepare()

measured. The default is approximate, so a node without an override can only disable optimizations that rely on the guarantee.

The accuracy of the tiled subtree, from the child’s and the window measured by

prepare(). With the band T, the value clipped to T is the minimum of every copy’s clipped value when the window covers every copy that can come within T of a point (a copy left out has its box farther than T, so its value is at least T by the child’s box promise). The minimum of L-Lipschitz fields is L-Lipschitz, and outside a finite array’s box every copy’s value is at least the per-axis distance to its own box, which lies inside the array’s. So:

  • approximate if the child is approximate, the window misses copies within the band, or the child was last prepared with a narrower band than this node;

  • the child’s accuracy and bound when no two copies’ boxes meet (disjoint copies: the nearest copy is the true distance to their union, inside and out);

  • otherwise a bound with the child’s Lipschitz bound (merged copies).

Returns:

The accuracy of the subtree rooted at this node.

class PolarArray : public Unary#
#include <polar_array.h>

Repeats its child N times around an axis.

Copy 0 is the child as authored. Without an angle range the copies are spaced 360 / N degrees apart around the axis (through center); with a range (start, end) in degrees they are spaced evenly from start to end inclusive, copy 0 rotated to start.

Evaluation is a pull-back: the point’s angle about the axis picks the nearest copy, the point is rotated back by that copy’s angle and the child is sampled there, so attributes follow the material. instance_index_field() exposes the copy index as a field, so material can vary per copy.

Neighbours: prepare() measures the child’s angular half-width w about the axis, and a point evaluates every copy whose angle lies within the window’s reach, ceil(w / step) plus a half steps (at least one neighbour on each side), of its own angle, taking the nearest. The reach is measured either way round the circle, so with an angle range the copies at the two ends also see each other across the empty part of the circle. Every copy whose material can hold the point is therefore evaluated. A child whose box reaches around the axis makes every copy a neighbour.

Attributes: sample() evaluates and returns attributes only where the value is <= 0.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy()): over a full circle the window always holds the nearest copy of an exact child, so it stays exact while copies stay apart and becomes a bound where they meet. A bound child, or an angle range, needs every copy left out of the window to be farther than the band, and a bound child also needs every copy turned by a multiple of 90 degrees about a coordinate axis; otherwise the value is approximate.

Bounding box: the child’s box swept around the axis (a bounding cylinder).

virtual DistanceAccuracy distance_accuracy() const override#

How faithfully this node’s value, including its whole subtree, matches the true signed distance.

Composes the node’s own operation with its children’s accuracy, so the root’s answer describes the whole tree. exact and bound promise that the value clamped to the bandwidth is lipschitz_bound()-Lipschitz and that values outside the bounding box are at least the per-axis distance to it (see DistanceAccuracy). Only valid after prepare(); some nodes decide from what prepare()

measured. The default is approximate, so a node without an override can only disable optimizations that rely on the guarantee.

The accuracy of the arrayed subtree, from the child’s and the window measured by

prepare(). The value is the nearest copy within the window. With the band T it keeps the child’s Lipschitz bound when the window holds, at every point, the copy with the smallest value clipped to T: the minimum of L-Lipschitz fields is L-Lipschitz.

  • Exact child, full circle: always. A copy’s material lies within the child’s angular half-width w of its own angle and the window reaches w plus half a step, so for the nearest material point of a copy left out, the window holds a copy that brings the same point at least as close (same circle about the axis, smaller angle).

  • Any child: when every copy left out of the window lies, angle-wise, farther from the point than the child’s box grown by T reaches about the axis; such a copy’s value is at least T by the child’s box promise. A copy left out lies at least the window’s reach from the point’s angle, either way round the circle (the window wraps across the empty part of an angle range), so prepare() checks that the grown box reaches less far round the axis than the window. An angle range needs it. The array’s box holds every turned copy’s box. An exact child’s value is at least the Euclidean distance to its box, so it keeps the box promise; a bound child only promises the per-axis distance, which survives only turns that map the axes onto the axes. So:

  • approximate if the child is approximate, the window can miss a copy, a bound child is turned off the axes, or the child was last prepared with a narrower band;

  • the child’s accuracy when the copies’ angular sectors are apart (the nearest copy is the true distance to their union, inside and out);

  • otherwise a bound with the child’s Lipschitz bound (merged copies).

Returns:

The accuracy of the subtree rooted at this node.

class Difference : public Binary#
#include <difference.h>

A difference binary node.

The difference is taken as the left child minus the right child.

Supports an optional blend (BooleanBlend) where the cut meets the left child: a radius, which may be a field, and a profile (quadratic by default, as with the original k constructors; circular, chamfer or cubic). A radius of 0 is sharp. The value is -smooth_min(-left, right). A smooth difference only removes material, so attributes come from the left child and the bounding box is the left child’s.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy(), for the whole subtree): never better than the weakest child. Both children are prepared at the bandwidth plus the blend’s support(), so the blend never reads a value the children do not promise. A sharp difference, and one blended with a constant quadratic or cubic radius, is a bound with the larger of the children’s Lipschitz bounds. Circular and chamfer profiles and field radii are approximations.

virtual DistanceAccuracy distance_accuracy() const override#

How faithfully this difference and its subtree match the true distance.

See the class description. The value is the (smooth) maximum of left and -right, clamped to the bandwidth T; with S the blend’s support() the children are prepared at T + S. A silent left child gives no value (left at least T + S, so the result is at least T). A silent right child returns the left child’s value unblended, which is what the blend gives for -right at or below -(T + S): blending with a value at least S beyond changes nothing while left is above -T, and keeps the clamped result at -T otherwise. Children’s values beyond T + S (for example where the cut goes silent deep inside the left child) are clamped away the same way, so the clamped value is a Lipschitz function of the children’s clamped values with their larger bound. The result is at least left, so outside the box it is at least the per-axis distance.

Returns:

The weakest of the children’s accuracy and the difference’s own.

class Intersection : public N_ary#
#include <intersection.h>

Intersection of two or more nodes, optionally blended where they meet.

The blend (BooleanBlend) is a smooth maximum: a radius, which may be a field, and a profile (quadratic by default, as with the original k constructors; circular, chamfer or cubic). A radius of 0 is sharp. The result does not depend on the order of the children. A smooth intersection only removes material, so every point inside the result is inside every child, attributes are combined as before, and the bounding box is the overlap of the children’s boxes.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy(), for the whole subtree): never better than the weakest child. The children are prepared at the bandwidth plus the blend’s support(), because a smooth maximum near the surface reads values up to support() beyond the bandwidth. A sharp intersection, and one blended with a constant quadratic or cubic radius (any number of children), is a bound with the children’s largest Lipschitz bound. Circular and chamfer profiles and field radii are approximations. Children whose boxes do not overlap give an empty box at the origin, so that case is an approximation too. A single child keeps its own accuracy.

If you call prepare() first and then clone the node, the clone() operation will copy from memory instead of re-reading from disk.

virtual DistanceAccuracy distance_accuracy() const override#

How faithfully this intersection and its subtree match the true distance.

See the class description. With T the bandwidth and S the blend’s support(), the children are prepared at T + S, and G_i (child i’s value clamped to [-(T + S), T + S], T + S where it is silent) is L_i-Lipschitz. The intersection returns no value where any child is silent, and clamping the (smooth) maximum of the raw values to [-T, T] gives the same as clamping the maximum of the G_i: a value at or above T + S keeps the result at or above T, and one at or below -(T + S) cannot move the clamped result (as a smooth minimum: blending a value with one at least S above it changes nothing, and once the sorted fold is above T, folding in a value at least S above T keeps it above T). The quadratic and cubic blends with a constant radius change by at most the largest change of their inputs, so the result keeps the children’s largest Lipschitz bound. The (smooth) maximum is at least every child’s value, so outside the intersected box it is at least the per-axis distance to that box, which also makes the box early-out continuous.

Returns:

The weakest of the children’s accuracy and the intersection’s own.

class BBoxIntersection : public N_ary#
#include <bbox_intersection.h>

An accelerated n-ary boolean intersection node utilizing an internal Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) tree.

This node drastically improves performance when sampling intersections of many spatially distinct children by only evaluating children whose bounding boxes overlap the sample point. 

    The value is that of a sharp Intersection: the maximum of the children's values, and no
    value where any child has none or is left out of the AABB query (more than the bandwidth
    outside its box). This node's own attributes are only evaluated, and attributes only
    returned, where the value is 0 or less.

    Bounding box: the intersection of the children's finite boxes (children with an infinite
    corner do not bound it); a point at the origin if those boxes have no common point.

    Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy(), for the whole subtree): as a sharp Intersection,
    a bound with the children's largest Lipschitz bound, never better than the weakest child.
    Children whose finite boxes do not overlap make it an approximation. A single child keeps
    its own accuracy.

class Union : public N_ary#
#include <union.h>

Union of any number of nodes, optionally blended where they meet.

The blend (BooleanBlend) has a radius, which may be a field, and a profile: quadratic (the default, and the behaviour of the original k constructors), circular, chamfer or cubic. A radius of 0 is a sharp union; a field radius blends only where it is positive. The result does not depend on the order of the children: the per-point values are sorted before they are folded.

Attributes: inside one or more children their attributes are combined as before (this node’s first, then the children’s, through the conflict resolvers). A blend also creates fillet material outside every child; there the two nearest children are sampled at their closest surface points and mixed by the blend weight (AttributeCombination::mix_attributes), so a fillet between two materials grades from one to the other. Attributes are only evaluated and returned where the union’s value is 0 or less.

Bounding box: the children’s boxes, padded by the blend’s max_dip() for one or two children. The sorted fold of three or more values can dip deeper than one blend, so with three or more each face is padded by how far the fold of the children’s gaps to it reaches, at most the support() (SmoothBlend::union_bounding_box()): one dip where a single child sticks out, more where several children end at the same face.

Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy(), for the whole subtree): never better than the weakest child. A sharp union is a bound (the minimum of exact distances is exact outside but only a bound inside overlapping children), as is a quadratic or cubic blend with a constant radius, for any number of children. A field radius scales the value, and circular and chamfer blends can be steeper than 1, so those are approximations. A single child keeps its own accuracy.

Subclassed by MappedStructureCollection

class BBoxUnion : public N_ary#
#include <bbox_union.h>

An accelerated n-ary boolean union node utilizing an internal Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) tree.

This node drastically improves performance when sampling unions of many spatially distinct children by only evaluating children whose bounding boxes overlap the sample point. 

    Bounding box: the children's boxes, padded as a quadratic Union with radius k: by k for one
    or two smooth children, and for three or more by how far the fold of the children's gaps to
    each face reaches, at most the support 4k (SmoothBlend::union_bounding_box()).

    Attributes: only evaluated and returned where the union's value is 0 or less: this node's
    own, then those of the children that contain the point.

    Distance accuracy (distance_accuracy(), for the whole subtree): as Union with a constant
    quadratic blend. Sharp or smooth, with any number of children: a bound, never better than
    the weakest child. A single child keeps its own accuracy.

enum class BlendProfile#

The cross-section of the fillet a smooth Boolean puts where two surfaces meet.

With r the blend radius, each profile dips below min(a, b) by at most max_dip() and only where |a - b| (or both values) are within support() of each other. Elsewhere the result is the sharp min.

Values:

enumerator quadratic#

The original smooth union: a polynomial fillet, dip r, support 4r.

The default.

enumerator circular#

A circular-arc fillet of radius r between perpendicular surfaces, dip (sqrt(2) - 1) r, support r.

enumerator chamfer#

A flat 45-degree bevel, dip r / sqrt(2), support r.

enumerator cubic#

A curvature-continuous (C2) polynomial fillet, dip r, support 6r.

class BooleanBlend#
#include <smooth_blend.h>

The blend a Boolean node applies: a radius (constant or field) and a profile.

Union, Intersection and Difference each hold one. A radius of 0 (or less) gives a sharp Boolean; a field radius may be 0 in some regions and positive in others, so the edge is only blended where the user wants it. A field radius needs known bounds so the node can pad its bounding box and its children’s bandwidth.

Distance accuracy: a sharp Boolean, or a quadratic or cubic blend with a constant radius, is a bound (the blend never has a slope above 1). Circular and chamfer blends can have a slope up to sqrt(2) where the surfaces meet at shallow angles, so they are approximations. A field radius with a Lipschitz hint L is divided by 1 + L and stays a bound for the quadratic and cubic profiles; without the hint it is an approximation.

DistanceAccuracy distance_accuracy() const#

How faithfully the blended value matches the true distance, for exact children.

The operation alone, for children whose values are true distances everywhere. The nodes’ Node::distance_accuracy() overrides compose it with their children’s accuracy, bandwidth and bounding box (see Union::distance_accuracy()).

Returns:

bound when sharp, or for a quadratic or cubic blend with a constant radius or a field radius with a Lipschitz hint; approximate otherwise.

inline bool is_sharp() const#

Returns true when the radius is a constant 0 or less, so every point is sharp.

Returns:

True when the radius is a constant 0 or less, so every point is sharp.

bool keeps_distance_bound() const#

True when a Boolean node can keep its children’s distance bound through this blend.

Sharp, or a constant radius with the quadratic or cubic profile. Then the blend of any number of values changes by at most the largest change of its inputs (each step of the sorted fold has non-negative partial derivatives that sum to 1), blending a value with one at least max_support() above it is the sharp minimum, and the sorted fold never ends more than max_support() below the smallest value (two values: at most max_dip() below). A field radius scales the value, and the circular and chamfer profiles have slopes up to sqrt(2), so those do not qualify.

Returns:

True if sharp, or a constant radius with the quadratic or cubic profile.

namespace SmoothBlend#

The one blend used by Union, Intersection, Difference and the lattices.

A smooth max is -smooth_min(-a, -b) and a smooth difference is -smooth_min(-a, b). Radius 0 (or less) is the sharp min. Every profile changes the value by at most 1 per unit change of the radius, so a field radius with slope bound L adds at most L to the result’s slope.

std::pair<glm::vec3, glm::vec3> union_bounding_box(const std::vector<std::pair<glm::vec3, glm::vec3>> &child_boxes, double radius, BlendProfile profile = BlendProfile::quadratic)#

A smooth union’s bounding box: its children’s combined box, each face padded by how far the blend can reach past it.

Outside its box a child’s value is at least the per-axis distance to that box, so at t past a face of the combined box each child’s value is at least t + g, g being how far the child’s box stops short of that face. The sorted fold never falls when a value rises, and the quadratic and cubic folds shift with their values, so the union’s value there is at least t + fold(gaps): the face is padded by -fold(gaps), clamped to [max_dip(), support()]. That reaches the support only where many children end at the same face, and stays one dip where a single child sticks out. The circular and chamfer folds do not shift with their values, so their faces get union_padding(count). The fold only deepens with the radius, so a field radius uses its largest.

Parameters:

  • child_boxes – The children’s bounding boxes.

  • radius – The blend radius; 0 gives the combined box.

  • profile – The fillet profile.

Returns:

The padded box, as min and max corners.

double union_padding(double radius, size_t count, BlendProfile profile = BlendProfile::quadratic)#

How far the smooth minimum of count values can reach beyond the sharp one, whatever the values.

max_dip() for one or two values. The sorted fold of three or more can dip deeper than one blend (three equal values: 1.5625 r for the quadratic profile), so it gets support(). That holds for every profile: material (a result of 0 or less) needs the smallest value below support(). For the quadratic and cubic profiles the fold also never ends support() or more below the smallest value: if the running result is e <= k below it (k the support), the next value is at least e above the result, so the step lowers the result by at most h(e) and the gap becomes at most e + h(e) <= k (h(e) = (k - e)^2 / (4k) for the quadratic profile, ((k - e) / k)^3 k / 6 for the cubic).

Parameters:

  • radius – The blend radius.

  • count – The number of values (children).

  • profile – The fillet profile.

Returns:

support() for three or more values, otherwise max_dip().
